dataset.name: C Programming Fundamentals
dataset.description: C basics, operators and control flow, pointers, arrays and strings, functions and dynamic memory, structs, unions and enums, and the preprocessor.

questions.question: Which header declares the printf function?
questions.explanation: stdio.h provides standard input and output functions such as printf and scanf.

questions.question: Where does the execution of a C program begin?
options: The first function in the file
questions.explanation: Every hosted C program must define main, which is where execution starts.

questions.question: C is a case-sensitive language, so Count and count are different identifiers.
questions.explanation: Identifiers, keywords and function names are all case-sensitive.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d", 7 / 2);
questions.explanation: Both operands are int, so C performs integer division and drops the fractional part.

questions.question: Every simple statement in C must end with a ______.
questions.explanation: The semicolon terminates a statement, for example int x = 5;.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%.2f", 3.14159);
questions.explanation: The %.2f format prints a floating-point number rounded to two decimal places.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%zu", sizeof(char));
questions.explanation: sizeof(char) is 1 by definition in C. The size of every other type is measured in units of char.
x / 2.0 is 2.5 because one operand is a double. The comparison 2.5 > 2 is true, which prints as 1.
A char is a small integer. 'A' is 65, adding 2 gives 67, which is the code for the letter C.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d", -7 / 2);
questions.explanation: Since C99, integer division truncates toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3 (not -4 as in floor division).
Unsigned arithmetic wraps around modulo 256 for unsigned char, so 255 + 1 becomes 0.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d", (int)3.99);
questions.explanation: Casting a double to int truncates the fractional part, it does not round.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d", 'a' < 'b');
questions.explanation: Character constants are integers. 'a' is 97 and 'b' is 98, so the comparison is true, which is 1.

questions.question: In C, the value 0 is treated as false and any non-zero value is treated as true.
questions.explanation: Conditions in C are integer expressions, and only zero counts as false.
/ gives the integer quotient (3) and % gives the remainder (1).

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%05d", 42);
questions.explanation: In %05d, the 0 flag pads with zeros and 5 is the minimum field width, so 42 becomes 00042.

questions.question: Which operator gives the memory address of a variable?
questions.explanation: The address-of operator & returns a pointer to its operand.
i++ yields the old value (5) which is stored in j, and then i is incremented to 6.
a += a * 2 means a = a + (a * 2), which is 6 + 12 = 18.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d %d %d", 6 & 3, 6 | 3, 6 ^ 3);
questions.explanation: With 6 = 110 and 3 = 011 in binary, AND gives 010 (2), OR gives 111 (7) and XOR gives 101 (5).

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d %d", 1 << 4, 64 >> 3);
questions.explanation: Shifting left by n multiplies by 2^n and shifting right by n divides by 2^n.
7 % 2 is 1, which is true, so the ternary operator picks the first string.
Without a break after case 1, execution falls through into case 2. The break in case 2 then stops it.
i is halved each time with integer division (10, 5, 2, 1), and the loop stops when it reaches 0.
The sum goes 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. The first time it exceeds 10 is when it reaches 15, then the loop breaks.

questions.question: In C, the single equals sign (=) tests whether two values are equal.
questions.explanation: = is assignment. Equality is tested with ==.
x = 5 assigns 5 to x and the whole expression evaluates to 5, which is non-zero and therefore true.
&& short-circuits: a++ yields 0 (false), so b++ is never evaluated. a still gets incremented, b does not.
The comma operator evaluates its operands left to right and yields the last one.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d", 2 + 3 * 4 - 6 / 2);
questions.explanation: Multiplication and division bind tighter than addition and subtraction: 2 + 12 - 3 = 11.

questions.question: The ______ statement skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves on to the next one.
questions.explanation: continue jumps to the next iteration, while break leaves the loop.
A do-while loop always runs its body once before checking the condition.

questions.question: What does a pointer variable store?
options: The memory address of another variable
questions.answer: The memory address of another variable
questions.explanation: A pointer holds an address, and you use * to access the value stored there.

questions.question: Which operator dereferences a pointer, giving access to the value it points to?
questions.explanation: *p reads or writes the object that p points to.

questions.question: A NULL pointer points to a valid object.
questions.explanation: NULL means the pointer does not point to any object, and dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.
p points to x, so assigning through *p changes x itself.
Pointer arithmetic scales by the element size. p + 2 points to the third int in the array.
Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them, not bytes.
The function receives the addresses of x and y and exchanges the values stored there, which is how C simulates pass-by-reference.
pp points to p, and p points to x, so two dereferences reach the value 5.
s + 1 points to the second character of the string, and * reads it.
sizeof(a) is the total array size in bytes (12) and sizeof(a[0]) is the size of one element (4), so the division gives the element count.
A pointer holds a memory address, which takes 8 bytes on a 64-bit platform regardless of the type it points to.
*p++ reads the value p points to (5) and then advances p to the next element, so *p now reads 6.

questions.question: What is a dangling pointer?
options: A pointer declared but never used
A pointer to memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope
questions.answer: A pointer to memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope
questions.explanation: Using a dangling pointer is undefined behaviour.

questions.question: A void * pointer can be dereferenced directly without casting it to another pointer type.
questions.explanation: The compiler does not know the size or type of the pointed-to object, so it must be cast first.

questions.question: The unary operator that gives the address of a variable is written with the symbol ______.
questions.explanation: &x produces a pointer to x.

questions.question: What does the declaration const int *p mean?
options: The int that p points to cannot be modified through p
Both p and the int are constant
questions.answer: The int that p points to cannot be modified through p
questions.explanation: Here the const applies to the int. A pointer that cannot be reassigned is written int *const p.
When an array has an initializer list that is shorter than its size, the remaining elements are set to zero.

questions.question: C checks array bounds at run time and throws an exception for invalid indexes.
questions.explanation: C performs no bounds checking. Out-of-range access is undefined behaviour.
strlen counts the characters up to, but not including, the terminating null character.
sizeof includes the hidden null terminator, so the array holds 5 letters plus '\0'.

questions.question: Which character marks the end of a C string?
questions.explanation: The null character is how string functions know where a string ends.
An array initialized from a string literal is modifiable, so the second character can be replaced.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d", strcmp("abc", "abc"));
questions.explanation: strcmp returns 0 when the two strings are equal.
strcat appends the second string to the end of the first (the buffer must be large enough).
m[1][2] is row 1, column 2, which is the last element of {4, 5, 6}.
The loop adds 3 + 5 + 7.
An array parameter decays into a pointer, so inside the function sizeof(a) is the size of a pointer (8), not of the whole array. 8 / 4 is 2.
p starts at the beginning of the array and is moved forward by one, so printing from p skips the first character.

questions.question: Modifying a string literal through a pointer, as in char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'X';, is undefined behaviour.
questions.explanation: String literals may be stored in read-only memory. Use a char array if you need to modify the text.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%zu", strlen("a\0b"));
questions.explanation: strlen stops at the first null character, which is the one embedded after the 'a'.

questions.question: Which standard function copies one string into another?
questions.explanation: strcpy copies the source string, including the terminating null character, into the destination buffer.

questions.question: The header ______ declares string functions such as strlen and strcpy.
questions.explanation: Include <string.h> to use them.

questions.question: Which function allocates memory dynamically on the heap?
questions.explanation: malloc(size) returns a pointer to a block of the requested number of bytes, or NULL on failure.

questions.question: Which function releases memory that was allocated with malloc?
questions.explanation: Every successful malloc should be paired with exactly one free.

questions.question: C passes function arguments by value.
questions.explanation: The function works on copies of the arguments. To modify the caller's variable you pass a pointer.
The function increments its own copy of the argument, so n in main is unchanged.
The dynamically allocated array stores the squares 0, 1, 4, so p[2] is 4.
calloc allocates memory and initializes all of it to zero, unlike malloc.

questions.question: What does malloc return when it cannot allocate the requested memory?
questions.explanation: Always check the returned pointer before using it.
The function multiplies n by the factorial of n - 1 until it reaches the base case.
A static local variable keeps its value between calls, so three calls return 1, 2 and 3.

questions.question: What is a memory leak?
options: Reading beyond the end of an array
Allocated memory that is never freed
questions.answer: Allocated memory that is never freed
questions.explanation: The memory remains reserved for the life of the program but can no longer be used.

questions.question: Calling free() twice on the same pointer is safe.
questions.explanation: A double free is undefined behaviour and can corrupt the heap.

questions.question: In a typical implementation, where are local (automatic) variables stored?
questions.explanation: Stack frames are created and destroyed automatically as functions are called and return.
realloc resizes the block and preserves the existing contents, so the first element is still 7.

questions.question: Memory obtained with malloc must be released with ______.
questions.explanation: free(p) returns the block to the heap.

questions.question: What is wrong with returning the address of a local variable from a function?
options: The variable no longer exists after the function returns, so the pointer dangles
Nothing, it is a common technique
questions.answer: The variable no longer exists after the function returns, so the pointer dangles
questions.explanation: The stack frame is gone after the return, so using the pointer is undefined behaviour.
f is a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning an int, and calling f(2, 3) calls add.

questions.question: Which keyword groups related variables of different types into one unit?
questions.explanation: A struct defines a custom data type with named members.
The two members are added: 3 + 4.
q points to p, and q->x = 10 modifies p's member x.
Enumerators are numbered from 0 by default, so BLUE is 2.
A = 5, B continues from the previous value to 6, and C is 7.

questions.question: What is characteristic of a union in C?
options: All members share the same memory location
Its members are always initialized to zero
Each member has its own separate memory
questions.answer: All members share the same memory location
questions.explanation: Only one member holds a meaningful value at a time, and the union's size is that of its largest member.
The union is as large as its largest member, the 4-byte int. The char shares the same memory.
The compiler inserts 3 bytes of padding after the char so that the int is aligned, giving a total size of 8.

questions.question: Assigning one struct variable to another of the same type copies all of its members.
questions.explanation: Struct assignment performs a member-by-member copy.
typedef gives the anonymous struct the name Box, so it can be used without writing struct.

questions.question: A C struct can contain member functions, as a C++ class can.
questions.explanation: C structs hold only data. You can store function pointers in them, but there are no member functions.

questions.question: The ______ operator (written with two characters) accesses a struct member through a pointer to the struct.
questions.explanation: p->x is shorthand for (*p).x.

questions.question: Which part of the compiler handles lines that begin with #, such as #include and #define?
questions.explanation: The preprocessor runs before actual compilation and performs text substitution.

questions.question: What does #include <stdio.h> do?
options: Inserts the contents of the header into the source before compilation
Links the standard library at run time
questions.answer: Inserts the contents of the header into the source before compilation
questions.explanation: The header provides declarations. The implementation lives in the C library.
The macro does plain text substitution: 2 + 3 * 2 + 3 = 2 + 6 + 3 = 11, not 25.
Parentheses around the parameter and the whole expression make the macro behave as intended.
MAX is replaced by 10 before compilation, so the expression is 10 * 2.

questions.question: A constant created with #define has a type that the compiler checks.
questions.explanation: It is only text substitution done by the preprocessor. A const variable does have a type.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%d %d %d", !5, !0, !!7);
questions.explanation: ! turns zero into 1 and any non-zero value into 0. Applying it twice (!!7) normalizes any non-zero value to 1.
The conditional operator is right-associative and 5 > 3 is true. The inner test 5 < 10 is also true, so the result is 1.

questions.question: What does the static keyword do when applied to a global variable or function?
options: Limits its visibility to the current source file
questions.answer: Limits its visibility to the current source file
questions.explanation: This is called internal linkage.

questions.question: Which function is the safe way to read a line of text from standard input into a buffer?
questions.explanation: fgets takes the buffer size and will not write beyond it. gets cannot limit the input length.

questions.question: The gets function was removed from the C11 standard because it cannot be used safely.
questions.explanation: gets has no way to limit the amount of input, which makes buffer overflows unavoidable.

questions.question: What does undefined behaviour mean in C?
options: The compiler always reports an error
The standard places no requirements on what the program does
questions.answer: The standard places no requirements on what the program does
questions.explanation: Anything can happen, including appearing to work, which makes such bugs hard to find.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%x", 255);
questions.explanation: %x prints an unsigned integer in lowercase hexadecimal.

questions.question:
What does the following C code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the standard headers included.)

printf("%o", 8);
questions.explanation: %o prints in octal, and 8 in base 8 is written 10.
